Accelerator neutron sources for X17 · an introduction · 21 Oct 2026

Fire protons at a light metal and it gives off neutrons. Lithium gives slow ones, which is what X17 needs. Beryllium gives mostly fast ones.

The principle behind Birmingham and FRANZ (lithium) and NPI Řež (beryllium), the (p,n) sources studied for MX17, and why the lithium ones come out ahead.

1

Details

This is a primer, not a new study. Every number comes from the dedicated feasibility studies in this repo (birmingham/, franz/, bepn_cyclotron/, lansce_wnr/, frm2_medapp/), whose slide notes are live on the site.

A correction to a common reading of the ranking: the sites at the top (Birmingham HF-ADNeF, FRANZ) use lithium, ⁷Li(p,n). The beryllium sources, ⁹Be(p,n) at NPI Řež and the Japanese BNCT cyclotrons, pass ATOMKI too but sit ×2.6 behind. Both work the same way, which is what the next slides explain, and the last slides show why the difference matters.

The neutron’s only job: be captured by ³He, slowly

what happens in the MX17 cell; hover the dotted words, points and shapes for details throughout

2

Details

MX17 fills a cell with ³He gas and sends neutrons through it. A captured neutron turns ³He into an excited ⁴He nucleus, ⁴He*. That nucleus gets rid of its energy, sometimes by emitting an electron–positron pair. The ordinary way (internal pair creation, IPC) gives pairs at all opening angles. If the X17 boson exists, some pairs come from X17 → e⁺e⁻ instead, and they all have a large opening angle: a bump on a smooth curve. The four MX17 arms measure the angle.

The neutron's energy matters because about ¾ of it goes into the helium (E* = 20.58 MeV + 0.75·E_n). ATOMKI saw its signal for helium formed at about 20–21 MeV, so the studies count X17 only from neutrons below 2.75 MeV. Faster neutrons still make pairs, but at a different helium energy, so they count only as background. They also cause trouble in the detector (slide 7).

That's why a neutron source for X17 should give as many slow neutrons as possible and few fast ones.

A proton swaps into the nucleus and pushes a neutron out

the reaction behind every source in this deck (lithium shown; beryllium works the same way)

Lithium: ⁷Li(p,n)⁷Be

costs 1.65 MeV, starts at 1.88 MeV

Birmingham (2.8 MeV), FRANZ (2.0 MeV)

Beryllium: ⁹Be(p,n)⁹B

costs 1.85 MeV, starts at 2.06 MeV

NPI Řež (18 MeV), Japanese BNCT cyclotrons (30 MeV)

3

Details

A light nucleus hit by a fast enough proton can absorb the proton and release one of its neutrons. For lithium: p + ⁷Li → n + ⁷Be. One proton in, one neutron out; the nucleus left behind has one more proton and one fewer neutron.

It isn't free. The products weigh slightly more than what went in, so the proton must bring at least that mass-energy (the "cost", −Q): 1.645 MeV for lithium, 1.851 MeV for beryllium. A little more than that is needed in practice (the threshold, 1.881 and 2.058 MeV), because some energy is always tied up in the motion of the whole system. Below the threshold: no neutrons at all.

Above it, whatever energy the proton has beyond the cost is shared between the neutron and the recoiling nucleus. The neutron, being much lighter, gets most of it. That one rule sets the whole story: how far above threshold you run sets how fast the neutrons are.

Other practical points: the target heats up (Birmingham puts ~80 kW on a rotating lithium target), and ⁷Be is radioactive, so a lithium target gets hot in both senses. Beryllium is a robust metal that takes high power.

Every MeV the proton has beyond the cost goes to the neutron

fastest neutron energy straight ahead, against proton energy, for the two reactions

lithium ⁷Li(p,n)

beryllium ⁹Be(p,n)

studied facility

4

Details

The curves are the textbook two-body result: a neutron emitted straight ahead (0°), leaving the daughter nucleus in its ground state. Each curve starts at the threshold and climbs nearly one-for-one: above a few MeV, an extra MeV of proton gives about an extra MeV of neutron.

Lithium sources live in the bottom-left corner. FRANZ plans 2.0 MeV protons (neutrons up to 0.23 MeV straight ahead), Birmingham runs 2.8 MeV (up to 1.10 MeV). Every neutron is in the useful window.

Beryllium sources are cyclotrons that run at 18–30 MeV, because that's what those machines are built for and where beryllium gives lots of neutrons. Straight-ahead neutrons then reach 16–28 MeV. You could run a beryllium target at 3 MeV, but it would give very few neutrons: the reaction is weak near its threshold, while lithium has a strong resonance right there.

The curve is the maximum. A real target gives a whole spread of energies below it (next slide), and beryllium also has break-up reactions (⁹Be → 2α + n) that add many neutrons at a few MeV.

A thick target gives a spread of neutron energies, not one

left: the proton loses energy as it ploughs in, making neutrons all the way down; right: Birmingham’s lithium spectrum for four beam energies

2.3 MeV protons

2.5 MeV protons

2.6 MeV protons

2.8 MeV protons

5

Details

High-current sources use a target thick enough to stop the protons. That gives the most neutrons per proton, but the proton loses energy continuously on the way in. At each depth it can still knock out a neutron, with the energy it has at that depth, until it falls below the 1.88 MeV threshold. So the source makes a spread from about zero up to the maximum of the previous slide.

The right panel is Birmingham's thick-lithium model (birmingham/bham_beam.py, normalised to the facility's quoted yield). Raising the beam from 2.3 to 2.8 MeV more than doubles the neutron output (1.7×10¹³ → 3.7×10¹³ n/s) and pushes the end point from 0.57 to 1.10 MeV. Still all slow, so the study picks 2.8 MeV.

The same happens in beryllium, from 18 MeV down to 2.06 MeV, so its spread runs across 0–16 MeV.

Lithium: all neutrons slow. Beryllium: most too fast

lithium (solid: Birmingham; dashed: FRANZ)

6

Details

Each curve is plotted as the share of neutrons per equal step in log-energy, so the area under a curve is proportional to the number of neutrons, and wildly different energies fit on one axis. Each is scaled to its own peak: this slide compares shapes, not how many neutrons each machine makes.

FRANZ (dashed) runs close to threshold: its neutrons are tens to a few hundred keV. Birmingham runs higher: up to 1.1 MeV, mean 0.56 MeV. Both are entirely inside the useful window.

NPI Řež at 18 MeV: mean 4.9 MeV, and only 42 % below 2.75 MeV. The bumps near 1.5 and 6 MeV are features of the nuclear-data evaluation (ENDF/B-VIII.0, sequential break-up through ⁹B and ⁸Be states); measured spectra are smoother, which doesn't change the fraction much. The study checked that the fraction is 31–48 % at every angle and beam energy: you can't steer around it.

Sources: birmingham/out/bham_spectra.csv, franz/out/franz_spectra.csv, bepn_cyclotron/out/bepn_spectra.csv (0–8° bin).

A neutron below ~1.7 MeV can’t fake an electron, so a lithium source never runs into this.

7

Details

MX17 decides to record an event when two arms each see a "leg": light in the SiPM wall and in the big plastic behind it, as an electron would make. A neutron above ~1.7 MeV can knock a proton out of the plastic hard enough to make that much light. A slow neutron can't.

Recording takes time: the DREAM electronics need ~0.3 ms per event, and during that time nothing else is recorded. With hundreds of thousands of fake legs per arm per second, random coincidences between arms keep the DAQ busy. At NPI Řež the study's best compromise turns the beam down to 0.63 of full current and still records only 45 % of the time. Birmingham doesn't need to turn anything down: 99 % live.

Numbers: Geant4 runs of the MX17 arms (the broad-band "soft" runs) re-weighted to each source, survey/soft_sim/out/soft_components.csv and bepn_cyclotron/out/bepn_components.csv. A faster DAQ (5 samples) or a higher leg threshold would help Be most; see the cyclotron study.

Neutrons fly everywhere: MX17 needs a wall with a hole

Without the wall, one arm would get

×113

Wall needed (estimate)

Be: ~1.0–1.2 m

Li: ~0.4–0.6 m

borated plastic (+ iron for Be)

8

Details

Unlike a proton beam, neutrons have no charge, so nothing can steer or focus them. They leave the target in every direction, somewhat more forward than backward (×3.3 for beryllium at 18 MeV; the lobe is drawn from bepn_cyclotron/out/bepn_angles.csv). The experiment takes a pencil of them through a Ø8 cm hole in a thick wall, 2 m away. Everything else must be stopped before it reaches the arms.

Fast neutrons are much harder to stop than slow ones, so the beryllium wall is about twice as thick. Both wall thicknesses are estimates: tenth-value layers and the detector's response to the leaking neutrons are stand-ins (bepn_shield.csv, bham_shield.csv). The Birmingham wall plus the room around it is the next thing to simulate in Geant4.

In practice, this means none of these sites can just put MX17 next to the target. Each one needs a port through a wall into a second room, which is one of the questions for each facility.

×N = ATOMKI X17/IPC (1.5×10⁻³) ÷ the 3σ reach in 50 days, big plastics, statistics + Geant4 background. Days: 50 × (reach/ATOMKI)².

9

Details

The figure of merit of all the studies: the smallest X17 signal (as a fraction of the ordinary pairs, X17/IPC) that a 50-day run would see at 3σ. ATOMKI's ⁴He claim corresponds to 1.5×10⁻³. Here it is turned into "×N past ATOMKI": ×2 means the run would see a signal half as strong as ATOMKI's. The note on each bar is how many days of beam would be enough to see ATOMKI's own signal (the reach improves as 1/√time).

Lithium at Birmingham and FRANZ: 3.3×10⁻⁴ and 3.3×10⁻⁴. Beryllium at NPI Řež: 8.7×10⁻⁴. Grey bars are the two non-(p,n) sources studied in the same way, for scale.

What the bars don't show: the arms need a port through a wall at every one of these sites, and none has offered one yet. FRANZ's number is for its design current, which it doesn't reach today. The verdicts and caveats are in each study's own slide note.

Three things to remember

Lithium near threshold is the natural X17 neutron source. Beryllium works, but pays for its fast tail.

1

Proton in, neutron out

A proton above threshold (1.88 MeV for Li) swaps into a light nucleus and knocks a neutron free.

2

Leftover energy = neutron speed

Run just above threshold (lithium, 2–3 MeV) and every neutron is slow, which is what X17 needs.

3

Fast neutrons cost twice

No signal, and they jam the trigger. Beryllium cyclotrons make 58 % of them.

What this primer leaves out: the room and wall around each target (not simulated yet); the 478 keV γ flood from lithium; whether any site can give MX17 a port through a wall; and FRANZ’s 2 MeV stage, which isn’t built yet. Each study’s slide note has the details.
